records.explanation: Von Neumann argues that once multiplication is available, other functions can be obtained from function tables with interpolation, so no further analytical operations need be built in. Division and square root are nevertheless included because their arithmetical procedures have about the same duration as multiplication and require only about a 50 percent increase in equipment. Cube root, logarithm, and trigonometric functions do not meet these specifications and are better handled by tables or power series under logical control. The list is a design decision about the boundary between built-in arithmetic and programmed computation.

records.explanation: Von Neumann defines the capacity unit as the ability to remember whether a stimulus was present at a given occasion, which represents one binary digit. A standard real number is fixed at 30 binary digits, keeping relative rounding errors below 2^-30, roughly 10^-9. Adding one unit for the sign and one to distinguish a number from an order gives 32 units per number. The memory is therefore subdivided into units and then into groups of 32 units called minor cycles, each holding exactly one standard number. Orders must also be formulated to occupy precisely one minor cycle. This organization simplifies synchronization and addressing: the digits of a number follow each other automatically, and the type marker in the first unit distinguishes numbers from orders. The 32-unit minor cycle is thus both a capacity accounting device and a structural unit of the code.

records.explanation: The 256 delay organs are numbered 0 to 255, and the 32 minor cycles in each are numbered 0 to 31. Because all organs are synchronized, minor cycles of a given number appear at the same time at all outputs. A minor cycle is completely defined by the pair µ, ρ. Von Neumann calls a delay organ a major cycle. A transfer of central control's connection to another minor cycle is permanent if control continues there, and transient if control must return to the original organ after the transfer. Number transfers between CA and M require abandoning the current connection and reestablishing it, so they are transient. He notes that every permanent transfer involves waiting on average half a transit through a delay organ, 512 periods τ, while a transient transfer involves two such waits, totaling one full transit of 1,024 periods τ. This addressing scheme is what makes a delay memory usable as a stored-program store.

records.explanation: Von Neumann compares the digits needed by each order type with the 31 available in a minor cycle. Operation orders need 5 digits, transfer orders need 13, and some need none. Pooling could save memory, but he limits it for three reasons: pooling should not require simultaneous operations, it should not upset timing, and it saves only instruction cycles, which are a small fraction of total memory. He therefore pools an operation order with the disposal of its result, since every disposal must be preceded by an operation and every transfer into CA must be followed by one. Transfer-in orders and control-transfer orders occur alone. The resulting seven order types use an average of about 50 percent of the 32 digits, leaving spare capacity for later changes. This is a concrete example of code design balancing memory efficiency against logical simplicity and timing constraints.

date.note: Section 11 of the 1936 paper; corrections published 1937.

records.explanation: Turing states that the results of §8 show the Hilbert Entscheidungsproblem can have no solution. He refers to Hilbert and Ackermann for the formulation and proposes to show there can be no general process for determining whether a given formula U of the functional calculus Z is provable. He distinguishes this from Gödel's results: Gödel showed there are propositions U such that neither U nor its negation is provable, whereas Turing shows there is no general method telling whether a given U is provable, equivalently whether Z with the negation of U adjoined is consistent. For each computing machine M he constructs a formula Un(M) whose interpretation is that 0 appears in some complete configuration of M. Lemma 1 shows that if 0 appears then Un(M) is provable; Lemma 2 shows that if Un(M) is provable then 0 appears. Hence a general provability decision process would decide whether M ever prints 0, which §8 shows impossible. Therefore the Entscheidungsproblem cannot be solved.

records.explanation: Turing first puts each machine table into a standard form in which every operation is one of a small set of forms such as erase-and-move or print-and-move. He numbers the m-configurations q1,...,qR and the symbols S0,S1,...,Sm, with blank as S0, 0 as S1, and 1 as S2. Each line becomes an expression like qi Sj Sk L qm, and all such expressions separated by semicolons form the standard description (S.D). Replacing qi by D followed by i copies of A, and Sj by D followed by j copies of C, and finally substituting digits for A, C, D, L, R, N, and semicolon yields an arabic numeral, the description number (D.N). The D.N determines the S.D and the machine uniquely; each computable sequence corresponds to at least one D.N, and no D.N corresponds to more than one computable sequence. Hence the computable sequences are enumerable. This encoding is what makes the universal machine and the diagonal argument possible.

records.explanation: Turing says the computable numbers include the real parts of all algebraic numbers, the real parts of the zeros of Bessel functions, and numbers such as π and e. He also says the computable numbers do not include all definable numbers and gives an example of a definable number which is not computable. Although the class is great and in many ways similar to the reals, it is nevertheless enumerable. The enumeration follows from the description-number encoding: each computable sequence corresponds to at least one description number, and no description number corresponds to more than one computable sequence. The non-computable definable number is the sequence P whose n-th figure is 1 or 0 according as n is or is not satisfactory; by the theorem of §8, P is not computable. Turing notes it may be possible to calculate any assigned number of figures of P, but not by a uniform process; when sufficiently many figures have been calculated, an essentially new method is necessary for more.

records.explanation: In the 1937 correction, Turing states that his proof of the insolubility of the Entscheidungsproblem contained some formal errors, and that other statements should be modified although not actually false as they stand. The expression for Inst{qi Sj Sk Lqo} is corrected, and the statement that Inst{qa Sb Sd Lqc} & F[n+1] implies CCn → CCn+1 is declared false even with the new expression, because one cannot deduce F[n+1] → (¬F(u,u'')) and therefore cannot use the term involving F(y',z) in Inst. To correct this, Turing introduces a new functional variable G, with G(x,y) interpreted as 'x precedes y', and defines Q as an abbreviation for a formula expressing the needed ordering properties. The corrected Un(M) is then (∃u)A(M) → (∃s)(∃t)RS1(s,t), where A(M) includes Q. With these modifications the proof is correct, and Un(M) can be put in the prenex form with n = 4. Turing acknowledges P. Bernays for pointing out the errors.
